---
title: "Norepinephrine isn't a fuel — it's a regulator"
description: "The brain chemical people call the alertness molecule does at least four jobs. That changes what a deficit would mean."
author: "Yannick Loth"
date: "2026-10-03"
categories: [Arousal system, Noradrenergic, Mechanisms]
---

Norepinephrine is usually introduced as the "alertness" or "fight-or-flight" chemical. That is true but incomplete. Norepinephrine is better understood as a *regulator* — a signal that adjusts how other systems behave — and it has at least four jobs that matter for ME/CFS.

**1. It sets arousal and sleep-state transitions.** Noradrenergic neurons in the locus coeruleus are active during wakefulness and quiet during sleep, and their activity sets the substates of non-REM sleep (@OsorioForero2021NoradrenergicNREM). Noradrenergic "microarousals" also sit at the centre of restorative sleep function (@Luthi2025MicroarousalsNoradrenaline).

**2. It drives the pumping that clears the brain.** During sleep, norepinephrine drives slow waves of blood-vessel movement (vasomotion) that push cerebrospinal fluid through the brain and clear metabolic waste (@Hauglund2025neVasomotion; @Nedergaard2026OscillatorySleep).

**3. It gates pain.** Descending pathways from the brainstem release norepinephrine in the spinal cord to damp pain signals (@Hayashida2019DescendingNoradrenergic). This is why drugs that raise norepinephrine are used for chronic pain.

**4. It helps supply fuel.** Norepinephrine stimulates astrocytes — support cells — to break down glycogen and release lactate, the fuel neurons burn (@Hertz2015neGlycogenolysis; @Killeen2013neLactate).

*Why this framing matters:* if the problem is a shortage of a fuel, you treat it by adding fuel. If the problem is a **regulator**, its failure shows up as disturbed sleep, poor clearance, pain amplification, and effort intolerance — and the fix is different.

*A caveat:* this is a useful reframing, not proof. The added roles come from animal and general studies; they have not been measured in ME/CFS.
